frameworks.name: Center of Influence (COI) Acquisition Model
frameworks.definition: A strategy that identifies gatekeepers and influential intermediaries as the primary customer, then systematically converts them into repeatable referral sources through deliberate customer experience design.

frameworks.name: Customer Chunking: Upstream vs Downstream
frameworks.definition: A mental model shift that reframes the business's primary customer from end-users to intermediaries (agencies, brokers, partners), enabling stable retention because intermediaries have structural incentives to stay while end-users are volatile.

frameworks.name: Broker Acquisition and Farming System
frameworks.definition: A two-pronged customer acquisition strategy for intermediaries: hunting (outreach to acquire new brokers) and farming (communication cadence and reciprocity-building with existing brokers to increase share of referrals from 10% to 100%).

claims.text: A building management agency (HOA for commercial properties) that has 147 accounts and 1.8M annual revenue can operate with only 90 minutes per week of founder work once systematized. This represents the annuity-stage of a service business where most development work is complete and primary constraint is founder effort allocation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: business maturity and founder hours required

claims.text: The primary bottleneck in growing a brokerage-dependent business (where word-of-mouth and broker referrals drive client acquisition) is not the client acquisition cost but the ability to scale brokerage relationships systematically. Without deliberate customer experience design and communication cadence, brokerage relationships plateau at low referral volume (e.g., 10% of potential referrals from any given broker).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B service business with gatekeeper-dependent lead generation
Brokers or COI partners as primary acquisition channel
claims.mechanism: Without systematic farming (regular communication and reciprocity-building), brokers see your business as one of many options, so they allocate only a small fraction of their referral volume to you. With deliberate activation and communication cadence, you can increase share of broker referrals from 10% (ad hoc) to 100% (systematic).
bounded_by: Assumes broker is motivated to refer (licensing rules prevent kickbacks, so motivation must come from reciprocity and relationship quality)
Does not apply to channels where customers have perfect information (e.g., transparent pricing, commodity services)

claims.text: Identifying the correct primary customer in a multi-stakeholder business is load-bearing to growth. Many service businesses mistakenly treat end-users as the primary customer when intermediaries (brokers, agencies, COI partners) should be. Once you reframe the business around intermediary retention and expansion, unit economics and retention rates improve dramatically because intermediaries have structural incentives to stay (they are themselves businesses) while end-users are volatile.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multi-stakeholder business where end-users are acquired through intermediaries
Intermediaries have structural incentive to stay (e.g., they are businesses, not individual consumers)
claims.mechanism: When you treat intermediaries as the primary customer and design product/experience/retention around their needs (not end-user needs), they develop reciprocal obligation to refer more business. End-users are volatile and churn for idiosyncratic reasons; intermediaries churn only if you fail to serve them well. This shifts the unit economics from 'maximize end-user LTV' to 'maximize intermediary lifetime value and share of referrals.'
bounded_by: Does not apply to direct-to-consumer businesses with no intermediaries
Does not apply if intermediaries are commodity brokers with no structural incentive to specialize in your service

claims.text: For a software platform (Allen) that white-labels to nail salons via agencies, the correct business model is to acquire agencies as customers, not nail salon owners directly. Agencies bring all their SMB customers and can offer platform access to many SMBs at once. SMBs leave agencies (causing customer churn at the platform level), but agencies rarely leave because they are businesses themselves and operate as stable entities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Software platform that white-labels via SMB-serving agencies
End-user SMBs are volatile and churn frequently

anchors.value: high churn (SMBs leave for various reasons)

bounded_by: Assumes agencies have natural incentive to keep platform (they white-label it to their customers)
Does not apply if SMBs have direct relationship with platform (direct-to-consumer SaaS)

claims.text: In broker-dependent service businesses, the cost of acquiring a broker (through outreach attempts) must be measured against the expected referral volume (e.g., 2-3 buildings per year per activated broker). Once you know the broker's expected lifetime referral volume, you can reverse-engineer the customer experience and activation process that accidentally worked with your first brokers and make it systematic.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Brokers send 2-3 deals per year once activated
claims.mechanism: By understanding the accidental customer experience that converted your first brokers, you can design a deliberate activation process (first touchpoint, communication cadence, value demonstration, reciprocity triggers) that converts future brokers at a predictable cost.

claims.text: For intermediary-dependent businesses, the primary marketing investment should be directed at the intermediary's customer journey, not the end-user's journey. This includes designing activation points, re-engagement campaigns, events, and communication cadences specifically for intermediaries to maintain top-of-mind awareness and reciprocal obligation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business model depends on intermediaries (brokers, agencies, COI partners) for customer acquisition
bounded_by: Does not apply to direct-to-consumer businesses

examples.text: A founder built a brokerage-dependent building management agency that grew to 147 accounts generating $1.8M in annual revenue with word-of-mouth and broker referrals. Initially, the growth felt like hitting brick walls repeatedly—no matter which direction he turned (pricing, positioning, new channels), he encountered obstacles. After systematizing the business, he now works only 90 minutes per week, but revenue stalls because broker relationships plateau at low referral volume (they send ~10% of their potential referrals). This exemplifies the founder bottleneck: the business is profitable and stable, but scaling requires systematic broker cultivation, not better sales mechanics or positioning.

A software platform (Allen) initially tried to sell directly to nail salon owners, positioning the platform as solving the salon owner's lead-generation problem. Salon owners loved the product ('this is amazing, it works') but had a follow-up question: 'How do I get leads?' The founder realized the platform solved leads *for* salons, not *how to get* leads into the platform—a mismatch. The founder then reframed: instead of selling to nail salons, he would sell to agencies that serve SMB nail salons. Agencies have leads (they run ads for their SMB clients), and agencies would white-label the platform to their customers. Once the upstream customer (agency) was correct, retention became stable: agencies never left because they are businesses, but SMB end-users (salon owners) churned constantly because they are volatile. This shift reorganized how the team thought about the business ('chunking up'), improving agency retention to near-100% while accepting SMB churn as structural rather than fixable.

A building management agency founder identified that all of his 147 accounts came from haphazard word-of-mouth, broker referrals, and property developers. When asked which brokers continue to refer, he noted 'all of them that have sent business in the past,' but the number was small. The founder then mapped the original broker relationships: What was the process from first contact to first referral? How frequently should he contact them to maintain top-of-mind? What reciprocity mechanisms (events, exclusive access, recognition) would increase their referral volume? This reverse-engineering revealed that his best brokers had received a deliberately designed customer experience—even though it was accidental the first time. The task was to systematize that experience for future brokers: clear activation point, consistent communication cadence, value proposition aligned with the broker's needs (not the end-user's), and explicit expectations about referral volume.

practices.text: For intermediary-dependent businesses, allocate 40 hours per week to broker/COI cultivation: reverse-engineer the process that led your original intermediaries to refer business, design deliberate activation and communication cadences, and measure the cost of acquiring each new intermediary against expected lifetime referral volume.

When entering a market with gatekeeper dependencies (brokers, enterprise procurement, government contracts), shift your mental model: brokers and COI partners are your primary customers. Design your entire go-to-market around their customer journey, not the end-user's. Ask: What's their activation point? What's their re-engagement cadence? What events or value propositions would make them want to refer more?

In multi-layer businesses (platform + agencies + end-users), 'chunk up' your thinking: acquire at the stable layer (agencies/intermediaries), not the volatile layer (individual SMBs). Measure intermediary retention separately from end-user retention, and optimize retention cadence around intermediary needs, not end-user needs.
